CHARLESTON, South Carolina (CNN)  -- Tropical storm Cristobal was forecast to move "parallel and very close" to the North Carolina coast Sunday morning, but the storm is not expected to make landfall along the eastern U.S. shores. Satellite image taken at 1:15 p.m. Saturday shows Tropical Storm Cristobal off the coast of the Carolinas. At 11 p.m. ET Saturday, the center of the storm was about 45 miles southeast of Cape Fear, North Carolina, and about 170 miles southwest of Cape Hatteras, North Carolina. The National Hurricane Center said Cristobal was moving northeast at about 6 mph, with maximum sustained winds of about 45 mph and some higher gusts. "The center of the tropical storm is expected to move parallel and very close to the coast of North Carolina for the next day or so," the NHC said. It is expected to dump between three and five inches of rain along the Carolina coast this weekend, it said. The storm had not strengthened beyond the 45 mph top winds measured earlier on Saturday, according to the NHC. A discussion posted online by NHC forecasters called Cristobal "convectively challenged" and predicted the storm would "become absorbed ahead of an approaching cold front" by late Monday. Although the center of the storm was forecast to remain off the coast through the weekend, tropical storm warnings were in effect from the South Santee River in South Carolina to the North Carolina-Virginia state line, including Pamlico Sound. Flood advisories were posted for coastal counties, and Wilmington, North Carolina, received 2½ inches of rain Saturday, said Stephen Keebler, a meteorologist at the National Weather Service there. Cristobal's winds were not expected to be a problem, Keebler said. "It's some rain and a little bit of relief for the coastal areas and a lot of excitement, but that's about it," he said. The rain bands were weakening as they spun farther inland, providing little relief for parched areas near Interstate 95 in North Carolina, he said. Forecasters predicted up to 5 inches of rain along the North Carolina coast, with heavier amounts in some areas. Eastern North Carolina is under a moderate drought, and areas along South Carolina's northern coast are considered abnormally dry, according to the U.S. Drought Monitor. Officials have blamed the persistent drought for a massive wildfire that has burned more than 40,000 acres in eastern North Carolina since it began June 1 with a lightning strike. As Cristobal lurked offshore, the storm was keeping many boaters off the waters -- and surfers in the waves. On North Carolina's Outer Banks, surfers reveled in the waves as the storm churned offshore well to the south. Bradley Rose, a surf instructor at SandBarz in Carolina Beach, North Carolina, said the waves were a bit choppy. "It looks pretty fun out there," Rose said. At the By the Sea Motel in North Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, out-of-state vacationers took to the beach, trying to photograph the outer rain bands of Cristobal, hotel manager Charlie Peterson said. Intermittent rain showers during the afternoon were not enough to chase them away, and there were even brief moments of sunshine. "They've got their cameras set, and they think there is going to be lightning over the water and all," he said. "They have never seen this." Elsewhere Saturday, Hurricane Fausto strengthened far off Mexico's Pacific coast, while Hurricane Bertha, located east of Cape Race, Newfoundland, was downgraded to tropical storm status. Neither of those storms currently threatens land. Bertha had blustered across Bermuda this week, knocking out electricity to thousands there.

In an online forecast discussion, NHC meteorologists described the storm as having difficulty sustaining convection. They expected it to be absorbed by an advancing cold front by late Monday.

Although Cristobal’s center was predicted to stay offshore throughout the weekend, tropical storm warnings covered the area from South Carolina’s South Santee River northward to the North Carolina-Virginia border, including Pamlico Sound.

Flood advisories were also issued for coastal counties. Wilmington, North Carolina, recorded 2½ inches of rain Saturday, according to Stephen Keebler, a meteorologist with the local National Weather Service office.

Keebler said Cristobal’s winds were unlikely to cause significant trouble. He characterized the event as mainly a rainmaker that would bring some relief to coastal communities and generate considerable interest, but little more.

As the storm’s rain bands moved farther inland, they weakened, offering scant benefit to drought-stricken locations near Interstate 95 in North Carolina, Keebler said. Forecasts called for as much as five inches of rain along the North Carolina shore, with locally higher totals possible.

While Cristobal remained offshore, it discouraged many people from taking boats onto the water but attracted surfers. On North Carolina’s Outer Banks, surfers enjoyed the swells created by the storm as it spun well to their south.

**WILMINGTON, North Carolina (CNN) —** Tropical Storm Cristobal tracked northeast just off the North Carolina coast, avoiding landfall but bringing heavy rain, gusty winds and dangerous surf to parts of the state.

The storm’s center was expected to remain over the Atlantic as it passed near the Outer Banks before moving farther out to sea, according to forecasters. Cristobal’s strongest winds stayed offshore, but coastal communities experienced squalls and occasional tropical-storm-force gusts.

Tropical storm warnings were posted for portions of the North Carolina coastline as officials urged residents and visitors to monitor forecasts. Forecasters said the main threats were heavy rainfall, localized flooding, high surf and rip currents rather than widespread wind damage.

Rainfall totals generally ranged from 2 to 4 inches near the coast, with isolated locations receiving around 5 inches or more. Lower amounts were reported farther inland. Ponding was possible on low-lying roads, though no major river flooding was expected.

The rain was welcome in a state struggling with drought conditions, particularly across eastern North Carolina. Agriculture officials said the moisture could help stressed crops and lawns, but cautioned that intense downpours can run off quickly and would not erase longer-term rainfall deficits.

Along the coast, residents secured outdoor furniture and kept an eye on tide levels, while emergency officials warned motorists not to drive through flooded roads. Many locals described the storm as more of a wet and windy disruption than a major emergency.

Tourists faced a different inconvenience. Red warning flags flew at several beaches, and lifeguards urged swimmers to stay out of the water because of strong currents and pounding surf. Some vacationers moved activities indoors, while others gathered along boardwalks and piers to watch the waves from a safe distance.

Even without landfall, forecasters warned that Cristobal could produce hazardous conditions well away from its center. Beach erosion and rip currents were expected to remain concerns after the storm moved away, and small-craft operators were advised to stay in port until seas subsided.

Conditions were forecast to improve as Cristobal accelerated northeastward into the open Atlantic.

# Cristobal Moves Northeast Off Carolina Coast, Bringing Rough Surf and Heavy Rain

**By Staff Writer**  
**Saturday, July 19, 2008 | 11:30 p.m. EDT**

**WILMINGTON, N.C.** — Tropical Storm Cristobal moved northeastward Saturday night over the Atlantic near southeastern North Carolina, producing bands of heavy rain, gusty winds and increasingly dangerous surf from Cape Fear toward Cape Hatteras.

The storm’s center remained offshore, limiting the threat of widespread wind damage. Nevertheless, forecasters warned that Cristobal could continue to affect beaches and sounds through Sunday with rip currents, locally heavy rainfall and periods of tropical-storm-force wind, particularly in exposed coastal locations.

In its late-evening advisory, the **National Hurricane Center** said Cristobal was moving generally northeast and was expected to follow a track roughly parallel to the North Carolina coastline. Forecasters emphasized that the storm’s strongest winds were primarily over water and on the system’s eastern side.

“Cristobal is expected to remain near or just offshore as it moves northeast,” the center said in advisory language, adding that residents should not focus solely on the forecast position of the center because rain squalls and hazardous marine conditions extended well away from it.

Radar images Saturday night showed curved bands rotating inland near Cape Fear and extending northeast toward the Outer Banks. Rain fell intermittently in Wilmington, Southport and communities along the lower Cape Fear River, while winds increased along oceanfront beaches.

## Conditions Deteriorate Along Beaches

At Wrightsville Beach, wind-driven rain swept across nearly empty streets as police monitored beach access points. Most visitors had left the sand by sunset, although small groups gathered under covered walkways to watch waves breaking beyond the pier.

“This isn’t shaping up like a major wind event for us, but it doesn’t take a hurricane to create life-threatening surf,” said **Laura Bennett, a fictional composite local meteorologist**. “The storm is moving alongside the coast, and that can keep the ocean agitated for an extended period. The rip-current danger may persist even after the rain begins to pull away.”

Forecasters said rainfall amounts would vary sharply because of the storm’s banded structure. One community could receive repeated downpours while an area only a few miles away remained comparatively dry.

Low-lying roads and locations with poor drainage were most vulnerable to temporary flooding. Officials urged motorists not to drive through standing water, especially after dark.

Near Carolina Beach, longtime surfer **Daniel “D.J.” Mercer, a fictional composite source**, watched the water from behind the dunes but said he had no intention of paddling out overnight.

“The waves look tempting from a distance, but the current is moving hard and the sets are disorganized,” Mercer said. “You can get pulled down the beach or out past the break before you realize what’s happening. Tonight is a night to watch, not ride.”

Beach patrol officials echoed that warning, saying tropical systems can produce powerful rip currents even when skies appear to improve between squalls.

## Hotels Prepare for Questions and Cancellations

Hotels along the Cape Fear coast reported a mix of cancellations, early departures and last-minute calls from travelers asking whether roads and bridges remained open.

“We’ve had guests standing in the lobby looking at the radar on their phones and asking whether they should leave,” said **Monica Ellis, a fictional composite front-desk manager at an oceanfront hotel**. “We’re telling everyone to follow emergency officials, stay off the beach after dark and keep balcony doors secured.”

Ellis said hotel workers had moved outdoor furniture, checked emergency lighting and placed towels near entrances where rain was blowing under doors.

Farther north, businesses on the Outer Banks were also monitoring Cristobal’s projected path. Although the center was still well to the southwest Saturday night, forecasters expected conditions near Cape Hatteras to worsen as the storm continued northeast.

Hotel employees there said the greatest concern was not necessarily structural damage but the possibility that rough surf, heavy showers and strong wind gusts could disrupt weekend travel.

“People hear ‘tropical storm’ and either panic or assume it’s nothing,” said **Aaron Price, a fictional composite hotel operations manager near Hatteras**. “The reality is in between. We’re staying open, but we’re taking the weather seriously and asking guests to do the same.”

## Cape Hatteras Could See Increasing Wind and Surf

The geometry of the North Carolina coast makes Cape Hatteras particularly exposed to storms moving northeast over the western Atlantic. Even if Cristobal’s center stays offshore, onshore wind could push water toward portions of the Outer Banks and produce overwash in the most vulnerable spots.

A **fictional composite Outer Banks meteorologist, Rachel Monroe**, said residents should prepare for rapidly changing conditions overnight and Sunday.

“Cristobal’s exact track matters, but the storm is not a single point on a map,” Monroe said. “Squalls can carry stronger wind to the surface, and the beaches could see dangerous breaking waves well before the center reaches its closest approach.”

Mariners faced some of the most significant hazards. Offshore winds and seas were expected to build around the storm, creating dangerous conditions for smaller vessels. Boaters were urged to remain in port and secure loose equipment.

The Coast Guard and local emergency managers advised residents and visitors to monitor official forecasts rather than relying on social-media images or assumptions based on conditions outside a single window.

## No Direct Landfall Needed for Hazards

Cristobal was not expected to become a major hurricane, but emergency officials stressed that weaker tropical storms can still cause injuries and localized damage through flooding, falling limbs, lightning and rough water.

The National Hurricane Center indicated that only modest strengthening was possible while Cristobal remained over warm Atlantic waters. The system was forecast to accelerate northeastward, eventually moving away from North Carolina.

For coastal communities, the timing meant the worst conditions could arrive overnight or early Sunday, when fewer people would be awake to notice rising water or unsecured objects.

Residents in flood-prone areas were advised to keep phones charged, secure trash cans and patio furniture, and avoid unnecessary travel during heavy rain. Visitors were told to check with local authorities before attempting to reach beaches, piers or ferry terminals.

By late Saturday, no broad evacuation orders had been issued. Emergency operations officials said they would continue tracking rainfall, wind and road conditions through the night.

Along the Cape Fear coast, the approach of darkness left the storm visible mostly through its sound: wind rattling signs, rain striking windows and waves breaking heavily beyond the dunes.

“Everybody wants to see what the ocean looks like during a tropical storm,” Mercer said. “The safest view is from well back.”
